media:group.media:title: The Waterloo series: Nassau
media:group.media:description:
The small duchy of Nassau had a relatively large impact on the battle of Waterloo compared to its small size, with its troops holding on in the most intensely disputed areas of the battlefield. Nassau was one of those small German principalities dragged along into a war by the larger powers. They had limited choice in which side to choose or for whom they would fight... but fight they did. The small duchy put its mark on the infamous battle where Napoleon was finally defeated.

media:group.media:title: The battle of Waterloo series: Brunswick
media:group.media:description:
Brunswick was the smallest nation present at the battle of Waterloo in 1815, fighting on the Allied side, under the direct command of the British. This video shows in detail where the armies were located on the Waterloo battlefield, and why Brunswick armies were there in the first place. The video also describes in detail the regiments and uniforms, and the historic background of the house of Brunswick and its army.

entry.title: I created the 1815 waterloo battlefield in 3d

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: I created the 1815 waterloo battlefield in 3d
media:group.media:description:
I am really excited that for the first time, I am able to go beyond the generic backgrounds I usually use to create scenes. In previous videos, I create accurate models of soldiers, weapons, and troopers with appropriate horse harnesses and blankets for cavalry, but the backgrounds are fairly generic. I usually think about them in terms of what type of terrain and background would be appropriate, e.g. are there mountains, forests etc … but after this, I create a background that works, using buildings appropriate for region and time setting (churches from a region etc).
The current model of a large 3d environment of the Waterloo battlefield, in terms of terrain, positioning of all buildings, streams, forests, orchards and crops etc, means I can create scenes and camera angles as they would be during the famous battle. I can place all troops across the total battlefield in the right number and locations and recreate their points of view (POVs). Waterloo is likely the easiest to this with, as there is a lot more information available compared to other battles. I therefore want to showcase my Waterloo battlefield here, which I will use for future videos and I hope to replicate this concept with other battlefields.

entry.title: The Battle of Waterloo, a good example of how not to fight a Napoleonic battle

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: The Battle of Waterloo, a good example of how not to fight a Napoleonic battle
media:group.media:description:
This video is my first venture into, what I consider, the difficult territory of the battle of Waterloo. It took me a bit longer to make this video, as it is almost completely animated with own material and I needed to make a whole new set of models, especially for the Brits. Forgive me that I have not included, Prussian, Dutch, Belgium, Nassau and Hanoverian army uniforms... I hope to make up for this in future videos.
I think Waterloo is such a difficult subject, as the battle stood for so much more than the actual bloody action itself. The final outcome of Napoleon's downfall was in my mind already a given. It was just a question if it would be a 100 days or 200 days, and what would be the further fallout in the immediate aftermath. It was not the empire defeating event as frequently described, as this defeat had already happened. This was not the Trafalgar on land, a defining moment when France stopped being able to compete with Britain at sea.
It was also a battle full of mistakes by two very good military commanders. Wellington was just praised as he was the commander on the winning side but a lot went wrong on both sides, causing enormous casualties. I tried here in 20 minutes to indicate what I thought went wrong and why. I know this will likely give a lot of opinions and comments, as Waterloo is one of the most plucked apart battles in terms of interest, angles and opinions details. I hope you enjoy it.

entry.title: The Crimean war, the Russians had no chance against the destroying angel, the Enfield P1851

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: The Crimean war, the Russians had no chance against the destroying angel, the Enfield P1851
media:group.media:description:
This video tells the history of the development fire arms from the smoothbore flintlock muskets, to the percussion musket, ending in 1854 with development of the percussion rifle. The Crimean war is the most well known example where this played out in the extreme, as percussion rifles of the English and the French would fight percussion smoothbore muskets of the Russians.

entry.title: The Charleville musket, the first mass produced fire arm in history, how it was made and works

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: The Charleville musket, the first mass produced fire arm in history, how it was made and works
media:group.media:description:
The French standard infantry musket of the French revolutionary and Napoleonic wars was the first fire arm that truly went into mass production to arm its massive conscript army. This was the first fire arm that was designed and build for mass production, with easy replacement and interchangeable parts to supply a massive field army. Caliber size was similar for all French hand fire arms. In this video I show how the Charleville was build from all its loose parts and how it worked.
I used two models for the animations downloaded from Sketchfab under free use license, many thanks for making them available:

entry.title: The light cavalry of Napoleon in 1805, leading the Grande Armée to victory at Austerlitz

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: The light cavalry of Napoleon in 1805, leading the Grande Armée to victory at Austerlitz
media:group.media:description:
The light cavalry of the Grande Armée of Napoleon formed the advance vanguard, allowing the army to move at record speed. They were responsible for scouting out the best routes in terms of food supply and enemy movement, supplying intelligence for optimal conditions to defeat the enemy. As such they formed an important component of the new way of warfare, being the eyes and ears of Napoleon in terms of information gathering and setting up the army.
Keywords: Napoleonic wars, Cavalry, Grande Armée, history, Austerlitz

media:group.media:title: Napoleonic Wars: Russian Army 1805, marching to Austerlitz
media:group.media:description:
Napoleonic wars in 1805, the Russians have signed a packed with Austria to attack emperor Napoleon Bonaparte. The Russian army had to be mobilised from around the Russian empire. I am indicating which regiments marched to Austria to attack Napoleon and where they came from. I have learned a few more animation techniques and I hope it shows. I equally started to use Midjourney videos, using old paintings as prompts to make the relevant historic figures come to live more. Let me know what you think. I hope you enjoy this video and many thanks for watching.

entry.title: The Austrian army in the Napoleonic age

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: The Austrian army in the Napoleonic age
media:group.media:description:
The Austrians can be considered a conservative Empire refusing to die, inferior in tactics to Napoleons' army, but with a superior strategy for long-term survival. The Austrian army remained flawed in its leadership but with highly skilled soldiers of every arm (infantry, cavalry, and artillery). Eventually the Austrians would be on the victorious side, and they can be considered the main enemy of the French and they lay the ground work for Napoleons demise.

entry.title: Napoleon's dragoons, the backbone of the cavalry arm

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: Napoleon's dragoons, the backbone of the cavalry arm
media:group.media:description:
Napoleonic wars, dragoons, cavalry, history
When discussing different army units and how they performed, most attention is given to the elite units, like the cuirassiers or guard units. However, the most numerous cavalry units of Napoleon were the dragoons. He increased their numbers dramatically and they provided the bulk of troopers for his most famous campaigns.

entry.title: Wunderwaffen, the wonder weapons, deciding wars in Europe in the 19th century

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: Wunderwaffen, the wonder weapons, deciding wars in Europe in the 19th century
media:group.media:description:
The idea of wonder weapons, as a deciding factor in war, has always been fascinating. We just have to look at the numerous of YouTube channels, creating simulation of old armies against a few new tanks or aircraft. The 1980 movie of the final countdown, seeing the USS Nimitz going back to 1941 is entirely based on just having the coolest fighter of its age, the F14 tomcat blow up a few Japanese zeros. We want to create our own wonder weapon histories. History has seen only a handful of real wonder weapons that truly tipped the balance in wars. I do think however there were a few in the 19th century during the time when development of fire arms went really quickly. Communication and exchange of technology between countries was slower, meaning that one country was able to be there first and thus use it in the next war with other countries. I therefore sum up three main examples that I consider relevant.
I am not the first one to mention them and they have been individually described in books and other YouTube channels. However, I think the historic timeline of mentioning them in historic succession is novel and useful, providing a good overview.
I consider the two world wars free of wonder weapons. Some might consider the tank for the Brits as one but the pro and con points have been argued enough, and I am firmly in the camp of not a wonder weapon. They were too early too soon, and by the time of the second world war came around, all larger countries had the relevant technology and playing field of tanks was relatively similar, we can argue about the nitty gritty of which tank was better (and some were truly better), but none were deciders in my mind.
Tell me what you think of my breakdown and if you disagree. Many thanks for watching and reading this!

entry.title: Empires and nation states in Europe, How the map of Europe changed in the last 250 years (Part 4)

author.name: Europe in the age of gun powder

media:group.media:title: Empires and nation states in Europe, How the map of Europe changed in the last 250 years (Part 4)
media:group.media:description:
This is the story of the map of Europe across the last 250 years. I am telling this story backwards, starting at the modern day and going back 250 years. I will indicate why the borders change in particular periods and how Europe came out of the age of Empire, moving back to nation states. I have tried to make the maps as accurate as possible, looking at as many sources as possible creating GIS shape files. Although the narrative had to remain relatively short to explain the transition, I attempted to create an overarching narrative explaining how we Europe was shaped and carries its past with it up to the current day.
This is part four, covering the map changes of Europe from 1854 to 1772
